cards.s: Experiment tracking and the model registry with MLflow
cards.html:
A gate answers "is this model good enough?". A registry answers "which model is in production, where did it come from, and what was there before?". MLflow records each training run (parameters, metrics, artefacts such as the model file) and keeps registered models with numbered versions.

src/credit_api/train.py:

cards.s: Experiment tracking and the model registry with MLflow
cards.html:
def log_to_mlflow(
    model: Pipeline, metrics: dict[str, float], params: dict[str, Any]
) -> None:
    import mlflow  # imported lazily: only needed with --track

    mlflow.set_experiment("credit-risk")
    with mlflow.start_run():
        mlflow.log_params(params)
        mlflow.set_tag("data_sha256", file_sha256(DATA_PATH))
        mlflow.log_metrics(metrics)
        mlflow.sklearn.log_model(
            model,
            name="model",
            registered_model_name="credit-risk",
            # MLflow 3 saves sklearn models with skops (safer than
            # pickle) and asks us to vouch for non-standard types
            skops_trusted_types=[TREE_PREDICTOR],
        )

cards.s: Experiment tracking and the model registry with MLflow
cards.html:
Every --track run creates a new version of the registered model credit-risk. Versions are labelled with aliases: @champion for the model in production and @challenger for the newest candidate. Code loads models:/credit-risk@champion, so promotion and rollback are just moving an alias.

Concept: Aliases replace the old "stages"

Older tutorials move models between the stages Staging and Production. MLflow deprecated stages in version 2.9 in favour of aliases and tags, because one fixed set of stages did not fit real workflows. If you meet stages in an existing project, the concept maps directly: Production ≈ @champion.

promote.py implements champion/challenger: the newest version becomes @challenger; if it passes the same gate against the current champion's metrics, it becomes @champion:

src/credit_api/promote.py:

cards.s: Experiment tracking and the model registry with MLflow
cards.html:
def main() -> int:
    client = MlflowClient()
    versions = client.search_model_versions(f"name='{NAME}'")
    newest = max(versions, key=lambda v: int(v.version))
    client.set_registered_model_alias(NAME, "challenger", newest.version)
    new = client.get_run(str(newest.run_id)).data.metrics

    try:
        champ = client.get_model_version_by_alias(NAME, "champion")
        baseline = client.get_run(str(champ.run_id)).data.metrics
    except MlflowException:
        print("no champion yet: the first model becomes champion")
        baseline = {}

    cfg = json.loads(THRESHOLDS.read_text())
    failures = check(new, baseline, cfg["floors"], cfg["max_drop"])
    if failures:
        print("challenger rejected:", *failures, sep="\n  - ")
        return 1
    client.set_registered_model_alias(NAME, "champion", newest.version)
    print(f"version {newest.version} is now @champion")
    return 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

cards.s: Experiment tracking and the model registry with MLflow
cards.html:
The weekly retraining workflow ties it together. A schedule trigger runs it every Monday; workflow_dispatch adds a manual button:

.github/workflows/retrain.yml:

name: Weekly retrain

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 3 * * 1"     # Mondays 03:00 UTC
  workflow_dispatch:         # plus a "Run workflow" button

# Only one run may write to the model registry at a time
concurrency:
  group: model-registry
  cancel-in-progress: false

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  retrain:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30
    env:
      # Real teams point this at a shared MLflow server; the fallback
      # keeps the tutorial runnable without one.
      MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI: >-
        ${{ vars.MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI || 'sqlite:///mlflow.db' }}
      MLFLOW_TRACKING_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.MLFLOW_TRACKING_TOKEN }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v10.3.3
        with:
          enable-cache: true
      - run: uv sync --locked --group tracking
      - name: Train and register a new model version
        run: uv run python -m credit_api.train --track
      - name: Promote to @champion if it beats the current one
        run: uv run python -m credit_api.promote
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        if: always()
        with:
          name: mlflow-db
          path: mlflow.db
          if-no-files-found: ignore

cards.s: Experiment tracking and the model registry with MLflow
cards.html:
Try it: See it locally

export MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI=sqlite:///mlflow.db, then run uv run --group tracking python -m credit_api.train --track twice (once with --max-iter 3 for a deliberately bad model), then uv run --group tracking python -m credit_api.promote after each. The bad model is rejected. Browse the runs with uv run --group tracking mlflow ui --backend-store-uri sqlite:///mlflow.db at http://localhost:5000.

Watch out: Where MLflow lives in a team

cards.s: Experiment tracking and the model registry with MLflow
cards.html: A SQLite file on a CI runner disappears after the job; our workflow uploads it as an artefact only so the tutorial works without a server. In a team, MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI points to a shared tracking server (self-hosted on ECS with a database and S3, or a managed offering such as Amazon SageMaker's MLflow), and the deploy pipeline exports models:/credit-risk@champion (export_champion.py) instead of training a fresh model.

cards.s: Closing the loop: which model is actually running?
cards.html: Be precise about what the tutorial setup does, because an interviewer will be. Without a shared tracking server, retrain.yml registers and promotes models in a SQLite file that disappears after the job. Its @champion never reaches production; deploy.yml trains its own model from the merged code. Both are legitimate designs, and you must be able to say which one you run:

cards.s: Closing the loop: which model is actually running?
cards.html:
Train-in-deploy (tutorial default)Registry-driven (MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI set)
Model in the imageTrained from the commit being deployed@champion, exported by export_champion.py
Quality gategate.py against baseline.jsonpromote.py, before the alias moves
A new model ships when…code or data changes are mergedretraining promotes a challenger and a deploy runs
Reproducible from Git alone?YesNo: needs the registry
Good forSmall models, few retrainsExpensive training, frequent retrains, several consumers of one model

cards.s: Closing the loop: which model is actually running?
cards.html: deploy.yml (lines 33–43) supports both: if the repository variable MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI is set, the build exports the champion instead of training. In registry mode, baseline.json should not be edited by hand any more: the champion's own metrics are the baseline, otherwise there are two sources of truth that will disagree.

cards.s: Closing the loop: which model is actually running?
cards.html: Lineage is the chain that lets you answer "what exactly is running?" in one minute during an incident:

cards.s: Closing the loop: which model is actually running?
cards.html:
Every link is recorded somewhere: Git, the data_sha256 tag on the MLflow run, the registry version, the image digest in the deploy job, the GitHub deployment history. train.py and export_champion.py write the part the service needs into models/model_meta.json, and /health reports it. This is real output with the exported champion:

expected output:

{'status': 'ok', 'version': '3f2a1c0', 'model_version': 'credit-risk/v1',
 'data_sha256': 'a7ad9a21934f'}

version is the code (git SHA), model_version the model, and data_sha256 the training data. Before this edition, the API reported the git SHA as model_version, which stops being true the moment models come from a registry.

cards.s: When to retrain: a decision table
cards.html:
"We retrain weekly" is a junior answer; a senior answer names the trigger and who decides:

TriggerUse whenWatch out
Schedule (our weekly job)Data arrives steadily; cheap trainingRetrains even when nothing changed; promotes noise unless the gate is paired (box above).
New labelled dataLabels arrive in batches (e.g. loan outcomes after 12 months)Label delay: the newest data has no labels yet.
Drift alarm (Chapter 7)Inputs shift, labels are slowDrift is a reason to look; retraining on drifted data can bake in a data bug.
Performance alarmLabels arrive quickly (fraud chargebacks)The best trigger when you have it; most credit models do not.
Code or feature changeAlways, through the normal PRAlready covered by CI.

cards.s: When to retrain: a decision table
cards.html:
Whichever trigger fires, promotion stays a gated decision, and for a credit model in the EU a human approval of the production deploy is a sensible default (Chapter 7 explains the regulatory side).

What if… the challenger was evaluated on newer data than the champion?

What happens: promote.py compares the challenger's metrics from its training run with the champion's metrics from its run. If the data grew between the two runs (new applicants arrived, so the split contains different rows), the two numbers come from different test sets. The challenger may "lose" against a champion that would score lower on today's data, or "win" for the same reason.

Why: Lesson 3 above: on 250 rows, the test set alone is worth ±0.06.

cards.s: When to retrain: a decision table
cards.html:
What you do: For promotion decisions, evaluate both models on the same, current test set, inside the promotion job: load models:/credit-risk@champion, score it on today's test split, score the challenger on the same rows, then apply the gate. This is called a paired comparison, and it is much more sensitive than comparing two numbers from different runs. Our promote.py keeps the simple version for readability; an exercise at the end of this chapter asks you to improve it.

What if… the new champion turns out bad in production?

cards.s: When to retrain: a decision table
cards.html:
What you do: Because code loads @champion, rollback is moving the alias back, one API call:

from mlflow import MlflowClient

MlflowClient().set_registered_model_alias(
    "credit-risk", "champion", "7"    # the previous good version
)

Note where the model is loaded. In our image-based setup, the model is baked in at build time, so moving the alias changes nothing until the next build and deploy: rollback = redeploy the previous image (Level 3). In a setup that loads @champion at startup, moving the alias and restarting the tasks is the rollback. Know which one your system is, before the incident.

cards.s: When to retrain: a decision table
cards.html:
What if… two retraining runs promote at the same time?

What happens: The schedule fires while someone clicks Run workflow. Both runs register a version, both set @challenger, and the "newest version" one of them promotes is not the one it trained.

What you do: One concurrency group for everything that writes to the registry. Our retrain.yml has it (lines 8–11): concurrency: {group: model-registry, cancel-in-progress: false}. And promote the version this run registered (MLflow returns it from log_model), not "the newest version in the registry".
